rationale: A wins because it keeps the dangerous inference in the open instead of turning it into the premise. A's "Chipotle won't raise prices this year — but won't say if the robots are why" is the honest story; B's "Chipotle bets a robot can hold the line on menu prices" writes the causal link before the proof exists. B is tighter, but tight wrong is still wrong.
gaps_in_A: "call it a pilot, not a rollout" is sharp but a little prosecutorial; the supplied fact says a 100-restaurant rollout, so the safer frame is scale skepticism, not semantic conviction.

"Digital Makeline's testing was disclosed alongside the Autocado rollout" and "coordinated strategy" stretch a thin fact. The update only says Chipotle is also testing it; no scope, result, or executive thesis is supplied.
"franchise-manager accounts" is sloppy for Chipotle and not grounded in the update. Ask for GM or store-level manager accounts instead.
"No clean hand-off yet" is too pessimistic. The operations angle around halved guac prep time is already pitchable to a trade reporter if Chipotle can provide methodology or kitchen access.
gaps_in_B: "Chipotle bets a robot can hold the line on menu prices" is the big sin. The update says prices are flat and automation is happening; it does not say the robot funds the freeze.
"automation as the implied offset" is still an inference, even if the set later admits it needs proof. Do not put inference in the headline and bury the caveat in the footnotes.
"the prevailing belief right now is that chains pass food-cost inflation straight to the menu" needs sourcing or softer framing. It may be true, but it is not in the supplied facts.
"they move to the counter" over-specifies "redeployed to the front line." Front line may mean customer-facing work, but the counter is your word, not Chipotle's.
